html:
Harness² Workbench has 641 unit and integration tests and seven end-to-end tests. Every one of them passed, many times over, on the 32-core workstation where it was built, including from a fresh clone. Then the repository got its first CI runs on GitHub's shared runners, which have two cores for a private repository, and the tests started failing: one per run, a different one each time, never the same one twice in a row.

A test that fails once is a bug until proven otherwise. Each of the four rested on an assumption that held only on a fast machine with stable file times, and one of them was hiding in production code. This post is how I found them, how I made my machine slow enough to fail the same way, and how I proved the fixes.

Making a fast machine slow

A shared runner is slow in two ways: few cores, and other work competing for them. Both are easy to reproduce on Linux:

# Two busy loops pinned to cores 2 and 3 ...
for c in 2 3; do taskset -c $c sh -c 'while :; do :; done' & done
# ... and the test binary pinned to the same two cores, run fifty times.
for i in $(seq 50); do taskset -c 2,3 ./target/debug/deps/<test-binary> --test-threads 8; done

Where two cores were not slow enough, one core with four busy loops was. The other half of the method was negative controls: a fix counts only if the old code fails under the same conditions and the new code passes. The first two fixes below have both numbers.

1. The exec race in /proc

The Workbench stops a crashed job's processes on restart only after identifying them: every step carries an H2W_JOB_ID marker in its environment, and the server reads /proc/<pid>/environ to find it. The test started sh -c "sleep 30 & exit 0" with the marker set, waited until every process in the group was named sleep, and asserted that each one carried the marker. On the first CI run it did not.

The reason is in the kernel's exec path. A process gets its new name early in exec, before the kernel has filled in the new program's environment pointers, and in between, /proc/<pid>/environ reads as empty. I measured it with a small script that spawns sleep and polls /proc at once: 260 of 500 spawns showed the name sleep with an empty environment, and it filled in after 0.018 ms at the median and 0.139 ms at worst. On a fast machine the test's first poll almost never landed there. On a two-core runner it did.

This was not only a test bug. Restart recovery read each process once, and an empty read meant "unmarked", so a job process caught mid-exec at the wrong moment would be left running. It fails safe (nothing unidentified is ever signalled), but it fails. The fix makes an empty read mean "look again": up to nine reads, with pauses doubling from 1 ms, about a quarter of a second in all, asynchronous so the server's runtime never blocks.

The first version of that fix was not enough, and the slow machine is what showed it. A new test catches processes mid-exec on purpose. Rust's Command::spawn returns while the child is still inside exec, so checking right after spawn lands in the window almost every time. Under load it still failed about one run in twenty. Two more windows explained it:

  • Permission denied. A child of a non-dumpable process inherits that flag until its exec marks it dumpable, and until then reading its environment fails with EACCES. The Workbench server is non-dumpable by design (it keeps same-user processes out of its own environment), and so is the test process once another test has exercised that code. From a small C program that marks itself non-dumpable and calls posix_spawn, 5 of 2,000 immediate reads were denied. Denied now also means "look again".
  • The parent's environment. A vfork-style spawn wakes the parent before the child's address space is switched, so a read at that instant can return the parent's environment, which in the test has no marker. I never caught this directly; it is the explanation that fits the failures that remained, and it matches the kernel source. In production it is harmless, because the parent of a job process is itself a marked job process. The test now waits for the new name before it checks.

With a single read, the new test fails on its first iteration, five runs out of five. With the fix, the /proc tests passed 100 runs out of 100 and the whole server unit suite 30 out of 30, all on two loaded cores.

2. The token bucket that refilled

The authentication tests send 500 requests with junk tokens and expect exactly 60 401 answers (the per-client limit) followed by 440 429s. On CI the count came back as {401: 61, 429: 439}.

The limiter is a token bucket, and a token bucket refills continuously. Sixty a minute is one a second, so any run that takes longer than a second earns an extra attempt. On one core with four busy loops the old test failed eight runs out of eight with exactly the CI numbers.

The fix is not to widen the assertion by a magic number. A helper computes what the limiter can have handed back over the measured run:

/// What a limiter of `per_minute` hands back over `elapsed`, rounded up.
fn refilled(per_minute: u32, elapsed: Duration) -> u32 {
    let ms = u64::try_from(elapsed.as_millis()).unwrap_or(u64::MAX);
    u32::try_from(u64::from(per_minute).saturating_mul(ms) / 60_000 + 1).unwrap_or(u32::MAX)
}

and the test accepts anything from the quota up to the quota plus that refill. Every downstream number (the 429 count, the metrics, the audit rows) now derives from the measured count instead of the constant. Four tests counted quotas this way; all four were changed, and the new file passed eight runs out of eight under the same load.

3. The browser test that read too soon

The end-to-end suite drives the real UI in headless Firefox. On one CI run it opened a finished job, waited for the log element to appear, read its text and did not find the line it expected. The element renders as soon as the job record arrives; the log lines are fetched after that. Locally the fetch always won.

Waiting for an element is not waiting for its content. A small helper now polls until the element contains the expected text, for up to 20 seconds, and puts the last text it saw in the failure message. Two other reads had the same shape: the experience-library view, and a diff that relied on a fixed 500 ms sleep. Both use the helper now, and the sleep is gone.

4. The order that came from file times

The last one was not about speed at all. A test copied a fixture experiment twice and compared the two experiments' sweep lists, in order. Sweeps are listed newest first, by the times of their files, and each copy got its own file times. On CI the two copies listed two sweeps in opposite orders. The test is about which sweeps are listed (one unreadable sweep must not hide the others), so it now compares them as sets.

Finding the rest before CI did

After the fourth fix I stopped waiting for CI to find the next one. I ran the whole workspace suite five times on starved CPUs: three runs on two cores with two busy loops, two on one core with two busy loops. All passed, and CI has been green since.

What I took from it:

  • Fast hardware hides timing assumptions. Every one of these passed every time locally. A shared runner is not a worse environment; it is a more honest one.
  • A test that fails once has found something. Three of the four were test bugs, each asserting something stricter than the system promises. The exec race was also a production bug that failed safe: it could leave a process running, but never signal the wrong one.
  • Build the slow machine yourself. taskset and a busy loop reproduce a two-core runner in seconds, and then the failure is yours to debug.
  • Wait for conditions, not for time, and derive tolerances from what you measured, not from a constant that happened to pass.
  • Prove a fix with a negative control. "It passes now" proves nothing about a race. "The old code fails 8 of 8 here and the new code passes 8 of 8" does.
